boards.title: Under-the-radar bottlenecks
boards.thesis: Find overlooked private startups with disclosed financing valuations around $100M or below across specialist AI, industrial technology, logistics, healthcare and climate. Explain the current external change creating demand, the specific company fit and the weakest link. Compare price evidence and downside. Larger comparisons may appear separately; never substitute funding amounts, SAFE caps or target prices for closed round valuations.

candidates.nicheReason: Kernel software for non-Nvidia accelerators is a narrow ecosystem bottleneck, not general AI.

tailwind.change: Big Tech is building custom AI chips, and chip rivals drew record funding in 2026.
tailwind.customerNeed: New chips need inference software stacks to run models.
tailwind.companyFit: Infinity says its Ignition agent generates stacks and kernels for non-Nvidia chips.
tailwind.weakestLink: Large chip owners may build software in-house rather than buy it.

candidates.rationale: Strongest price sourcing in the set: a company release plus TechCrunch. It is a specialist chip-software niche with a sourced sector change.

valuation.label: $100M post-money, company-stated and press-reported; instrument type unspecified

candidates.priceReason: The mark sits at the $100M preference ceiling on an unknown instrument. The ARR amount is undisclosed, so no multiple can be assessed.
candidates.bullCase: Alternative-chip makers need inference software stacks. Infinity's agent could serve many chip vendors.
candidates.bearCase: Hyperscalers may build stacks in-house. Its only public partner, d-Matrix, is far larger, creating concentration risk.
candidates.killCriterion: No second named chip partner or paying customer outside d-Matrix.
candidates.nextProof: Independent benchmarks and disclosed instrument terms.

company.name: Infinity (infinity.inc)
company.description: AI infrastructure research company whose Ignition agent generates inference software stacks and kernels for non-Nvidia AI chips.
company.alignment: Software-ecosystem bottleneck for alternative AI accelerators; a specialist rather than a general AI vendor.
strengths: Company-stated $100M post-money, independently reported
Named chip design partner d-Matrix (company and press)
company.uncertainty: Sits at the $100M preference ceiling. Instrument basis unknown. ARR amount undisclosed and benchmarks self-reported. Valuation is a historical mark, not an available price.
company.funding: $15M seed at $100M post-money (July 2026, company-stated; instrument unspecified)

candidates.nicheReason: AI digital workers for freight quoting, dispatch and documents form a specialist logistics niche.

tailwind.change: New 2026 seed rounds fund freight-agent startups; a weak blog survey suggests an adoption gap.
tailwind.customerNeed: Freight operators seek automation of manual back-office tasks.
tailwind.companyFit: Cargofy says it connects agents to existing freight tools and has operated since 2017.
tailwind.weakestLink: Adoption pace is uncertain, and the survey source is unverified.

candidates.rationale: Freight back-office automation with a longer operating history. The price is unconfirmed, so this is a diligence lead.

valuation.label: About $50M, per Axios unnamed source; basis unknown, company unconfirmed

candidates.priceReason: The approximate, anonymously sourced mark has an unknown basis. Round size is not valuation, and traction figures are first-party.
candidates.bullCase: If the claimed revenue and customers verify, the reported mark could look modest for an operating business.
candidates.bearCase: Nexcade and Freight Hero target similar work. Headquarters conflicts across sources, and traction is unaudited.
candidates.nextProof: A priced Series B or company confirmation of the valuation basis.

candidates.nicheReason: On-site visual AI for pallet verification at warehouse docks is highly specific.

tailwind.change: No sourced external change is in the admitted pool.
tailwind.customerNeed: Warehouses may need automated dock verification, but this is unsourced.
tailwind.companyFit: Company marketing describes dock units that read labels, count cases and detect damage.
tailwind.weakestLink: The why-now driver is entirely unsourced.

candidates.rationale: Narrow dock-verification niche at a small reported mark. The mark is stale and unconfirmed, so this is an unpriced lead.

candidates.priceReason: The approximate mark is anonymous and historical. PitchBook shows no valuation, and Tracxn conflicts. A small mark does not prove value.
candidates.bullCase: Dock counts and damage checks are a concrete, narrow warehouse pain point.
candidates.bearCase: The mark is stale and anonymous, and traction is unquantified.
candidates.killCriterion: No priced round or quantified pilot results.
candidates.nextProof: A named, company-confirmed financing with stated terms.

tailwind.change: No sourced external change is in the admitted pool.

tailwind.companyFit: Reports describe expansion across India after the HBF India seed.
tailwind.weakestLink: Both the demand driver and traction are unverified.

candidates.rationale: Very small company-sourced mark with weak commercial proof and a weak fit to the bottleneck theme.

candidates.priceReason: A tiny company-sourced mark with no basis or round size. Low price alone does not indicate value.

candidates.bearCase: Traction is unverified, reports trace to one release, and CB Insights investor data is inconsistent.
candidates.killCriterion: No independently verified patient or revenue traction.
candidates.nextProof: Stated round terms and verified usage data.

candidates.nicheReason: Agent deployment into industrial operations is a specialist vertical, though not small.

tailwind.change: The lead investor's marketing claims industrial firms run on legacy software.
tailwind.customerNeed: Industrial operators may need workflow automation across fragmented systems.
tailwind.companyFit: The company describes a model-agnostic platform with embedded teams and value-based pricing.
tailwind.weakestLink: The change is sourced only to investor marketing.

candidates.rationale: Larger comparison at about 1.4x the preference. It is included for contrast, not as an overlooked pick.

valuation.label: $140M post-money, CEO-reported to Fortune; not independently confirmed; larger comparison

candidates.priceReason: The CEO-attributed mark exceeds the $100M preference for a 2026-founded company with five claimed customers.
candidates.bullCase: Industrial firms on legacy systems may pay for outcome-linked AI deployments.
candidates.bearCase: Forward-deployed delivery may not scale, and consultancies and Palantir compete.
candidates.killCriterion: No repeatable deployments beyond forward-deployed engineers.
candidates.nextProof: Customer-verified production outcomes and confirmation of the valuation.

company.name: Arrakis

strengths: Official domain retrieved
Reported Series A led by Blossom Capital
Founded 2026 by a former Accel investor with a team from Palantir and others

output.summary: The search found only one named specialist with a sourced closed-round valuation: Arrakis, at $140M post-money in July 2026. That is above the $100M preference, so it is a labelled larger comparison. No qualifying company at or below $100M was found with a retrieved official domain. Other leads have no disclosed valuation or only an unnamed-source estimate, so they stay unpriced.

findings.title: Arrakis: larger comparison, not a qualifying small mark
findings.detail: Arrakis's $30M Series A was reported at $140M post-money in July 2026, per its CEO to Fortune. The $38M is total funding, not valuation. $140M is 1.4x the $100M preference. Company traction claims are unaudited.

findings.title: Demand change, customer need and weakest link
findings.detail: Fortune reports consultancies and Palantir racing into industrial AI. The need is agents that work with legacy industrial systems without replacing them. Weakest link: whether a forward-deployed, services-heavy model scales beyond five claimed customers against larger rivals.

findings.title: Small-mark gap and unpriced leads
findings.detail: No company at or below $100M had a confirmed closed-round valuation plus a retrieved official domain. LuminX's roughly $30M figure comes from an unnamed source, dated June 2025. Duvo's Series A shows no valuation. Both are unpriced leads.

output.summary: Browserbase operates in a crowded, rapidly commoditising cloud-browser market. At least six credible direct competitors — Steel, Browserless, Hyperbrowser, Kernel, Anchor Browser, and TinyFish — each lead on a distinct axis (open source, speed, stealth, auth, pricing, or full-workflow). Raw-session pricing is converging: Steel's managed cloud is $0.08–$0.10/hr versus Browserbase's $0.10–$0.12/hr, with self-hosted Steel eliminating metering entirely. Browserbase's defensible position is not the runtime but the Stagehand SDK (5.78M downloads), SOC 2/HIPAA compliance, session observability, and a nascent orchestration layer (Director, Agent Identity, MCP). One contested benchmark suggests Browserbase task success rates of 40–50%, materially below enterprise-grade expectations — unverified but material if substantiated. The durable commercial thesis requires SDK-to-paid conversion and orchestration attach rates that remain unverified.

events.message: Browserbase operates in a crowded, rapidly commoditising cloud-browser market. At least six credible direct competitors — Steel, Browserless, Hyperbrowser, Kernel, Anchor Browser, and TinyFish — each lead on a distinct axis (open source, speed, stealth, auth, pricing, or full-workflow). The durable commercial thesis requires SDK-to-paid conversion and orchestration attach rates that remain unverified.

original.summary: Browserbase is the best-funded pure-play cloud browser runtime for AI agents ($67.5M raised, $300M post-money valuation). The strongest bull case rests on three independently verified pillars: (1) Stripe-corroborated revenue at scale (hundreds of millions of session-minutes/month billed to hundreds of customers); (2) Stagehand SDK distribution moat (5.78M npm downloads, 25K+ GitHub stars) that creates switching cost independent of raw-session pricing; and (3) a founder with operationally traceable headless-browser expertise across Twilio → Stream Club → Mux → Browserbase. The revised thesis is not a managed-infrastructure pricing story but an SDK-distribution and agent-orchestration platform story. Steel's June 2026 repricing narrows the managed-session price gap to ≤$0.02/hr, confirming raw-session commoditisation is active. The durable advantage lies in Stagehand lock-in, SOC 2/HIPAA compliance, and a nascent orchestration layer (Director, Agent Identity, MCP) — products where open-source substitutes are absent. What must be true for this thesis to hold: Stagehand achieves meaningful free-to-paid conversion, enterprise contracts include minimum-commit ACVs, and orchestration products achieve material attach rates. These remain unverified.

previousOutput.revision: The Bear's falsifiability argument is structurally correct: Stagehand is MIT-licensed, explicitly marketed as usable without a Browserbase account, and carries zero licensing fee. This confirms the SDK cannot enforce conversion — it relies on developer preference and infrastructure convenience. However, the claim that the moat 'collapses entirely' is too strong: usagepricing.com discloses >$3M revenue and 1,000+ customers at June 2025 Series B, implying some conversion is occurring. Getlatka's $4.4M ARR estimate (July 2025) directionally corroborates this. The Model Gateway's API-key consolidation (browsers + search + fetch + models in one integration) represents a genuine but unquantified stickiness mechanism beyond raw SDK downloads. The load-bearing unknowns — free-to-paid conversion rate, gross margin, orchestration attach rate, enterprise ACV floors — remain unverified. Verdict: the moat exists but its durability and magnitude are unverified. 'PARTIALLY SUPPORTED' is the correct status: the Bear correctly identifies the falsifiable gap; the Bull correctly identifies that some revenue conversion is occurring.

events.message: Resuming the Investment Committee using the completed research and recorded verification.
Investment Committee started its resumed assessment.

After five research passes (scout, causal, hunter, founder, competitive, bear, verifier, bull revision), the Browserbase investment committee assessment reaches a MONITOR decision at MEDIUM confidence. What survives: real revenue triangulated at ~$4–5M ARR (mid-2025), genuine SDK developer distribution (~1.69M weekly downloads), Stripe-corroborated billing at scale, a credible founder with traceable domain expertise, and a documented multi-product stack (Model Gateway, Director, Agent Identity). What remains unverified and thesis-critical: free-to-paid conversion rate, gross margin on managed sessions, enterprise ACV floors, and orchestration-product attach rates. The $300M valuation at ~68x mid-2025 ARR is defensible only if those unverified links are material. Raw-session commoditisation by Steel is empirically confirmed. The thesis is a plausible platform story requiring verification, not a confirmed moat.

reviewNotes: Independent source-quality audit: omit the 5.78M download figure and its publication date because the historical measurement period has not been independently established. A current weekly download count cannot prove an earlier monthly or cumulative count. Stripe is a commercially interested vendor customer story: aggregate revenue and billing activity do not prove SDK-to-paid cohort conversion. GetLatka and pricing-blog revenue numbers are historical unaudited third-party estimates; do not present them as current verified ARR or derive a valuation multiple. Quoted session prices do not measure realised margins; self-hosting has operating costs. Public founder biographies do not establish a cap table or absence of other equity holders. Investor customer lists are interested claims, and Stripe billing integration does not establish that Stripe buys browser automation. Do not assert that competitors lack compliance capabilities from a comparison article. Keep these as explicit unknowns, and base the memo on the verified customer-attribution correction, the official Stagehand no-account requirement, and conditional next diligence actions.

Final evidence-quality constraint: the earlier draft still repeats unsupported metrics. OMIT all Stagehand download quantities and publication dates because the historical period was not validated. OMIT ARR estimates and derived valuation multiples; historical third-party estimates are not current audited ARR. OMIT claims of empirical margin compression: list prices do not measure margins, and self-hosting is not free. Aggregate vendor-reported revenue does not establish SDK cohort conversion. Do not describe investor/vendor customer lists as independent financial audits, or claim competitors lack compliance capabilities. Retain the real Contrary customer-attribution correction and official Stagehand MIT/no-account evidence. Describe developer distribution and willingness to pay as hypotheses. Return a concise qualitative decision with clear unknowns and concrete diligence actions. No false numerical precision.
